name: Urticaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach the tiny green flower + one-ovuled achene plan and the spring-loaded stamens, while making stinging hairs a Urtica clue rather than a family requirement.

project_scope.selection_mode: Central Texas family-first module across Boehmeria, Parietaria and Urtica
project_scope.note: The three local project genera are ideal for teaching the most important caution: Boehmeria and Parietaria are non-stinging nettle-family members.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Start with tiny greenish flowers in axillary/spikelike clusters. In staminate flowers, the filaments are commonly bent inward in bud and snap outward at opening; pistillate flowers have one ovule and mature as a small achene. Then use stinging hairs, leaf arrangement and stipules for genus.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Mostly herbs in the local pool. Leaves simple, alternate or opposite; stipules present or absent. Cystoliths are common. Stinging hairs occur in Urtica but are absent in local Boehmeria and Parietaria.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers are tiny, usually unisexual, commonly 4–5-part. Stamens match the tepal number and are often inflexed in bud, springing outward at anthesis. Pistillate flowers have a single 1-locular ovary with one basal ovule.
family_diagnostics.fruit: A small one-seeded achene, sometimes tightly enclosed by persistent perianth/bracts.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Do not ask 'does it sting?' first. Ask: tiny green flower clusters + explosive stamens + one-seeded achene; then split stinging Urtica from non-stinging Boehmeria/Parietaria.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: tiny green inflorescence → inflexed/explosive stamens → one-ovuled achene → stinging-vs-nonstinging genus doors → Rosales comparison
visual_lesson.intro: The nettle family is bigger than stinging nettles. Two of our three project genera do not sting, so the flower-and-achene machine matters more than pain.

steps.title: 1 · Find the tiny flower clusters
steps.look_for: Many tiny greenish flowers grouped in axillary clusters, spikes or cymose units.
steps.why_it_matters: Moves the ID away from generic serrated-leaf gestalt.

steps.title: 2 · See the spring-loaded stamens
steps.look_for: Four or five filaments bent inward in bud, then reflexing outward as the flower opens and ejecting pollen.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a memorable family mechanism and a stronger clue than stinging hairs.

steps.title: 3 · Confirm the one-seeded achene
steps.look_for: Single ovary with one basal ovule maturing into one small achene.
steps.why_it_matters: Separates the local nettle-family fruit plan from Moraceae multiple fruits and Euphorbiaceae 3-part capsules.

steps.title: 4 · Urtica door: the actual stinging nettle
steps.look_for: Stinging hairs plus opposite serrated leaves; handle visually rather than by touch.
steps.why_it_matters: Stinging hairs are useful once family is known, but they are not a family-wide requirement.

steps.title: 5 · Boehmeria door: false nettle without the sting
steps.look_for: Opposite or nearly opposite serrated leaves, no stinging hairs, and spikelike flower clusters.
steps.why_it_matters: This is the best local demonstration that 'nettle family' does not equal 'stinging.'

steps.title: 6 · Parietaria door: alternate, entire, stipule-free
steps.look_for: Non-stinging herb with alternate entire leaves, no stipules, and compact axillary flower clusters.
steps.why_it_matters: It looks unlike the stereotype yet retains the Urticaceae reproductive plan.

comparisons.title: Urticaceae vs Moraceae
comparisons.rule: Both can have tiny unisexual flowers. Local Urticaceae is herbaceous and produces individual achenes; local Moraceae is woody, latex-bearing and produces fleshy multiple fruits.

comparisons.title: Urticaceae vs Cannabaceae
comparisons.rule: Celtis is woody and produces drupes; local Urticaceae is herbaceous with tiny clustered flowers and one-seeded achenes.

comparisons.title: Urticaceae vs Euphorbiaceae
comparisons.rule: Stinging hairs can occur in both lineages. Urticaceae has ordinary tiny perianth flowers and a one-seeded achene; Euphorbiaceae uses a usually 3-carpellate ovary/3-part capsule, with Euphorbia using a cyathium.

visual_lesson.caveat: Stinging hairs, opposite leaves and stipules all vary within Urticaceae. The reproductive suite—tiny flowers, inflexed stamens and a single-ovule achene—is the safer family lesson.

diagnostic_photo_handoff.note: Family photo needs: bent stamens in bud vs open, female achene, Urtica stinging hairs vs Boehmeria, Parietaria node, Moraceae fruit comparison.
diagnostic_photo_handoff.verified_anatomy_only: Do not infer unseen structures from existing photos.

genera.fast_cue: non-stinging + opposite/nearly opposite serrated leaves + spikelike flower clusters
non-stinging + alternate entire leaves + stipules absent + axillary clusters
stinging hairs + opposite serrated leaves + tiny clustered flowers

teaching_cautions: Do not touch a suspected nettle to test the identification.
Do not teach stinging hairs as a family requirement; Boehmeria and Parietaria in the project are non-stinging.
Parietaria lacks stipules, so stipules are not universal in the family.

visual_targets.structure: inflexed stamens in bud / reflexed at anthesis

visual_targets.annotation_goal: label ovary, ovule and mature achene
label bulbous base and brittle tip without encouraging contact
non-stinging false nettle vs stinging nettle
show entire leaf + absent stipule + axillary cluster
